products.name: Waterfall plot
products.purpose: Show GEO longitude over time so parked, drifting and converging objects are visible at a glance. The primary situational product for the GEO belt.
must_contain: Most recent observations at the bottom
Payloads annotated; rocket bodies and debris removed or greyed unless relevant
Minimum of five days of data
Plus or minus three degrees either side of the primary object of interest
HRR 0, 1 and 2 payloads, Known Objects and UCTs highlighted and annotated
Annotations at the top of the waterfall where able
products.reads_as: Time runs down the page with the newest data at the bottom. A vertical trace is an object holding a longitude. A sloped trace is an object drifting, and the steeper the slope the faster the drift. Two traces converging to a point is a longitudinal crossing. A trace that changes slope has manoeuvred. A trace that stops sloping and goes vertical has stopped drift and parked.
common_misreads: Reading the plot upside down because a provider put newest at the top, inverting every drift direction
Interpreting a converging pair as a close approach when only longitude has converged and the objects remain separated in inclination
Missing a slope change because the plot window is too short; five days is the minimum for a reason
Treating an annotated debris trace as a payload of interest
products.request_phrasing: Request a waterfall covering the primary object, plus or minus three degrees, minimum five days, payloads annotated.

products.name: TRIC plot
products.purpose: Visualise relative motion between two or more objects in the Radial, In-track and Cross-track frame, so an RPO geometry can be read and characterised quickly.
must_contain: Clear depiction of relative motion and separation as a function of time
Relative distances in kilometres, or metres where appropriate
Individual RIC component separations and the total relative distance
Start and end points of the plotted period identified
Point of Closest Approach clearly indicated with relative distance and contributing RIC components at POCA time
Primary object clearly distinguished from secondary objects
Notations for important events such as start, end and TCA
Solar Aspect Angle information and Earth eclipse periods
Consistent colour system across pre and post manoeuvre TRICs
products.reads_as: The origin is the primary object; you are riding on it. Radial is up and down from Earth centre, In-track is along the direction of motion, Cross-track is out of plane. A closed ellipse traced once per orbit with a roughly two-to-one in-track to radial ratio is a natural motion circumnavigation. An ellipse that walks along the in-track axis is a drifting NMC. A shape that changes at discrete points is forced motion and each change is a manoeuvre. A side-to-side wobble once per orbit is a cross-track offset.
common_misreads: Reading a drifting NMC as a stable NMC because the drift is slow across the plotted window
Assuming a small total separation implies intent when the geometry is natural and unforced
Ignoring the eclipse and solar aspect angle bands, then being surprised when optical data gaps appear
Confusing forced motion with a poor orbit solve when the colour changes are not labelled as manoeuvres
products.request_phrasing: Request a TRIC for the primary against the secondary, with POCA annotated and RIC components at POCA.

products.name: Residual plot
products.purpose: Verify that an object is still on its element set, or reveal that it is not. The primary manoeuvre-detection product.
must_contain: At least seven days of observations at event opening
Observations preceding and during the manoeuvre for any closer view
Human readable residuals allowing in-plane or out-of-plane discrimination, either normalised time and beta, or right ascension and declination
No residual ratios
products.reads_as: Observations sitting on the zero line mean the current observations agree with the current orbital state. A departure from zero means the object is no longer where the state says it should be, which means it manoeuvred. Which residual type departs tells you the direction: an in-plane departure suggests a period or in-track change, an out-of-plane departure suggests a cross-track change affecting inclination or RAAN. Once a new solve is fitted the observations return to the zero line.
common_misreads: Calling a manoeuvre on a single outlying observation rather than a sustained departure
Missing that the state itself is stale, so the departure is epoch age rather than a manoeuvre
Reading a departure as verified when the provider has labelled it possible
Failing to notice observation density collapsed before the departure, so the fit is weak rather than the object moved
products.request_phrasing: Request a residual plot, seven days minimum, human readable residuals, with verbiage on whether it suggests a plane or period change and a bracketed manoeuvre time.

products.name: Photometric plot
products.purpose: Display light curves for a satellite and highlight anomalies suggesting attitude change, instability, deployment or breakup.
must_contain: Minimum of seven days of overlaid photometry
An additional view supporting validity: sensor view, extended view of fourteen to thirty days, or hemisphere view to remove hemispheric bias
Verbiage confirming the solar equatorial phase angles where the change was observed
Verbiage confirming the magnitude of the change
Neighbourhood at the time of change
products.reads_as: Visual magnitude plotted against time or phase angle. Remember that lower magnitude means brighter. A stable object produces a repeatable curve at a given phase angle. A periodic variation that was not there before indicates tumbling or attitude loss. A discrete step change indicates a configuration change such as a deployment or separation. A large sudden brightening can indicate a breakup, because many new surfaces are now reflecting.
common_misreads: Attributing a brightness change to the object when it is a phase angle effect, which is why the phase angles of the change must be stated
Attributing a change to the object when only one sensor saw it, which is why the sensor view exists
Attributing a change to the object when it is hemispheric bias, which is why the hemisphere view exists
Reading a gap in the curve as a change, when it is a collection gap or solar exclusion
products.request_phrasing: Request photometry, seven days overlaid, plus a sensor or hemisphere view, with the phase angles and magnitude of the change stated.

products.name: Neighbourhood
products.purpose: List the objects around an object of interest with the orbital and tasking context needed to assess who is at risk and who is behaving oddly.
must_contain: NORAD IDs, SOB and HRR rank where applicable
Latest state epoch time for each object
Source of the state, provider or Space-Track
Times and distances of close approaches
Inclination and delta to the object of interest
RAAN and delta to the object of interest
Longitude, drift rate and direction as appropriate
Constraints used stated on the product or in verbiage
No distance to closest approach filter applied; constrain by inclination and RAAN instead
products.reads_as: A table of who is nearby and how nearby. Read the epoch column first: a stale state makes every distance in that row questionable. Then read inclination and RAAN deltas, because small deltas mean plane matched, which is the expensive and therefore deliberate condition. Longitude and drift rate tell you whether the geometry is closing or opening.
common_misreads: Trusting a close approach distance computed from a state that is days old
Working only from an HRR-filtered neighbourhood and therefore missing an unranked object that mattered
Reading a small distance as significant when the planes are widely separated, so the objects pass quickly and never linger
Missing that a distance filter was applied by the provider, hiding the objects outside it
Reading only the originating provider in the source column and missing the pathway the state arrived by, when reconciling a discrepancy between two rows
products.request_phrasing: Request a neighbourhood constrained by inclination and RAAN, not by distance, with epoch ages and state sources, in both HRR-plus-UCT and HRR-only views.

products.name: COCO table
products.purpose: Identify co-orbital and co-planar relationships for LEO objects, indicating how readily one object could plane match with another.
must_contain: Primary compared against all payloads within the orbit regime
No distance filter, so constraints are plane related only
raDot and days to RAAN closure based on a nodal crossing normalisation
Constraints used highlighted at the top of the table
Inclination delta to primary
RAAN delta to primary, normalised or propagated
Coplanar angle or delta plane between the two objects
Age of state used for each object
Association status band per pairing, from same, close, nearby or none
Band threshold definitions stated in the header, four thresholds per band
Sustained close approach possible, as a true or false judgement per pairing
Nodal crossing delta
Days to right ascension zero
products.reads_as: A ranking of who could reach whom cheaply, and who could then stay. Read the band definitions in the header first, because association status is a banding against configurable thresholds rather than a physical property. Then read the sustained close approach possible column, which answers directly whether a pairing could linger rather than merely pass. Then use days to right ascension zero as a countdown and the right ascension rate to confirm the planes are closing rather than opening.
common_misreads: Ignoring days to RAAN closure and therefore missing a slow, deliberate, low-fuel plane match in progress
Reading a large current RAAN delta as safety when raDot is closing it rapidly
Assuming a distance filter is present, so treating an empty table as an all-clear
Reading an association status without knowing what the bands were set to on that run
Treating association status and sustained close approach possible as the same judgement; they are independent
Reading zero in the days to right ascension zero column as alignment, when it can equally mean no convergence is occurring
Treating the primary's self-comparison row as a duplicate rather than as a sanity anchor
products.request_phrasing: Request a COCO for the primary against all payloads in regime, no distance filter, with raDot and days to RAAN closure.

products.name: Pass schedule
products.purpose: Show when sensors can see the object, so collection can be planned and gaps anticipated.
must_contain: LEO covering an eight hour period; GEO covering a twenty four hour period
Two views: grouped by source or provider, and grouped by phenomenology
Time of next pass and provider
Time of next apogee and perigee
Time of next ascending and descending node
A present-time marker on the timeline
Node, apogee and perigee crossings marked against the timeline rather than listed separately
Sensor site identification sufficient to judge geographic and hemispheric spread
products.reads_as: A timeline of collection opportunity, one row per sensor or provider. Locate the present marker first or the schedule is only a list. Bars are pass windows and the gaps between them are the absence of coverage. Because sensor rows identify their sites, this is also the product that shows how much genuinely independent geography is covering a period, which is what decides whether a photometric change can be corroborated at all.
common_misreads: Planning against sensors that are not currently providing observations to the UDL
Reading a dense schedule as good coverage when it is all one phenomenology and therefore one failure mode
Missing that solar exclusion or eclipse will suppress optical passes that appear on the schedule
Reading density as diversity, when many passes from one hemisphere is a single failure mode
Planning against a pass that has already gone, by not locating the present marker
products.request_phrasing: Request a pass schedule grouped by provider and by phenomenology, with next pass, apogee, perigee and node crossings.

products.name: Post manoeuvre DC table
products.purpose: State the before, delta and after of a verified manoeuvre in a consistent format so crews read it the same way every time.
must_contain: Initial, Final and Delta columns, in that order
Time, Period, Longitude, Longitude drift rate, SMA, Perigee, Apogee, Inclination, Eccentricity, RAAN and Argument of Perigee rows
Accompanying standard verbiage with time of manoeuvre, delta-v, period change, perigee change, apogee change, inclination change and current drift rate
Clear labelling as possible rather than verified where the manoeuvre is not confirmed, with a stated confidence level
products.reads_as: Read the Delta column first, then ask which burn direction produces that signature. A change in period, eccentricity and possibly argument of perigee points to in-track. A change in eccentricity and argument of perigee alone points to radial. A change in inclination or RAAN points to cross-track. The drift rate row tells you where the object is going next.
common_misreads: Treating a possible manoeuvre DC table as verified because the format looks identical
Reading a small inclination delta as a cross-track burn when it is solve noise
Reporting the delta-v without stating the confidence or the supporting phenomenology
products.request_phrasing: Request the DC table in standard format with the standard verbiage block, and state whether possible or verified with confidence.

products.name: Ephemeris file
products.purpose: Provide a series of state vectors where an element set cannot represent the trajectory, notably for xGEO and hyperbolic transfers.
must_contain: Reference frame stated
Series of state vectors: epoch, X, Y and Z position, X, Y and Z velocity
products.reads_as: A table of where the object is and how fast, at a sequence of times, in a named frame. Used where a two-line element set cannot work because a trans-lunar injection has eccentricity greater than one and is therefore not an orbit at all.
common_misreads: Assuming the frame without reading it, which silently introduces a frame error of kilometres or worse
Attempting to fit an element set to a hyperbolic trajectory
Treating a sparse ephemeris as precise between its points
products.request_phrasing: Request an ephemeris file with the reference frame stated explicitly.

products.name: Gabbard diagram
products.purpose: Characterise a debris cloud by plotting apogee and perigee altitude against orbital period, revealing the breakup and its epoch.
must_contain: Apogee and perigee altitude for each fragment against orbital period
Parent object marked
Epoch of the data stated
products.reads_as: Each fragment appears twice, once as an apogee point and once as a perigee point. The characteristic crossing X pattern centres on the parent orbit, and the spread of the arms indicates the energy of the event. A tight cluster is a low energy shedding; a wide spread is an energetic fragmentation.
common_misreads: Reading early sparse fragment data as the full cloud, and therefore underestimating the event
Confusing a genuine debris cloud with a cluster of poorly correlated tracks
Assuming symmetry means a collision when a low energy anomaly can look similar early on
products.request_phrasing: Request a Gabbard diagram for the fragment set with the parent orbit marked.
